summary:
The Republic of Tyva (Tuva) stands under the national framework of Russia, and no division-specific transgender evidence appears in the source inventory for this republic. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (June 2025) contains no information specific to Tuva beyond that national framework, and the Human Rights Watch enforcement data is likewise national. A trans visitor is therefore assessed against the countrywide regime as it operates in Tuva.

Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned. Putin signed the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents in 2023, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year. The Supreme Court of Russia designated the international LGBT+ movement an 'extremist' organisation in November 2023.

The expanded 'propaganda' law criminalises public expression, explicitly including anything 'justifying' gender transition. Fines for individuals under these statutes reach 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or 15 days' detention, and foreigners who violate them face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation. Official national government warnings tell LGBT travellers of this exposure, and the US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement in Russia. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 'extremism'-related convictions for participation in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its symbols as of 30 June 2025, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison; it also documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media. Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Enforcement has grown in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. The Guardian reported on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as 'a second-class citizen' after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed 'Ada', a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

The UK Home Office note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
tangentialFactors:
No source in the inventory reports on transgender law enforcement, police practice or violence within the Republic of Tyva itself. The national pattern is documented in detail, but the geographic distribution of the 101 extremism convictions and the 98 administrative cases is not stated, so the share attributable to Tuva is unresolved.

Chechnya is the only Russian republic named in the sources, and it appears in the context of refugee protection rather than as a comparator for local conditions. Whether conditions in Tuva diverge from the national baseline in either direction is not sourced.

The conversion-therapy case documented by BBC Russian occurred near Novosibirsk, and the bar raids reported by The Guardian occurred in Moscow. Neither is evidence about Tuva, and neither should be read as a description of conditions there; they are cited as documented instances of the national regime in operation.

The trajectory of the national regime is one of expansion: an eighteenfold rise in propaganda-law cases over a decade, an extremist designation followed by raids within 48 hours, and a healthcare and document-recognition ban enacted in 2023. A visitor should expect the framework in force at the time of travel to be stricter, not looser, than the one described here.
localsOnly:
Residents of Tuva are barred from legal gender recognition: the 2023 law prohibits gender reassignment surgery and any change of gender marker on official documents, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year. There is no lawful domestic route to either.

Residents face the same exposure as visitors under the propaganda statutes, with individual fines up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or 15 days' detention, and under the extremist designation, which carries up to 12 years in prison for participation in or display of symbols of the designated movement.

Administrative liability under article 20.3 has been applied predominantly to online conduct: Human Rights Watch documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement nationally.

Residents have no access to gender-affirming care within the country, and the documented conversion-therapy case shows that family-initiated confinement and forced hormone administration can occur without effective protection. The UK Home Office position that LGBT+ people in Russia constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention is the standard applied to UK asylum claims, and Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those leaving.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Tuva-specific reporting on raids, arrests, extremism charges or violence against transgender people is present in the inventory. Whether any of the 101 extremism convictions or the 98 administrative cases were brought in Tuva is unresolved and not sourced.

The inventory does not state how Tuva's regional authorities, courts or police forces apply the national regime in practice, nor whether local prosecution rates differ from the national average. This is an absence of evidence, not a finding of leniency.

Local facility availability, documentation practice at airports and border crossings within Tuva, and access to legal representation or appeal for detained foreigners are not sourced. The Level 4 travel advisory and the warnings directed at LGBT travellers are national-level instruments; their specific application at Tuva's entry points is not documented.

The death in pretrial detention reported by the Associated Press in December 2024 and the conversion-therapy confinement reported by BBC Russian in July 2024 are single documented cases from other parts of the country. No equivalent case from Tuva appears in the sources, and none should be inferred.
